title: Has anyone actually managed to build a full game using ONLY AI in 2026? Looking for your stories and workflow tips.
author: AggravatingBee8744
selftext:
I am completely new to game development, but I’ve always wanted to bring my game ideas to life. Naturally, I immediately turned to AI.  
Since I’m a student on a budget, I’ve been looking into free alternatives like **DeepSeek**, **Gemini**, and **Qwen** (honestly, Qwen feels like the absolute best free LLM out there right now). I tried building projects both in pure HTML and using the **Godot Engine**. However, every single time, the AI eventually started losing track of its own code. Everything just ended up as a primitive prototype, leaving the game stuck in its infancy.  
I’d love to hear your stories about making games with AI for personal projects. Have you actually managed to ship a complete, polished game, or is AI still not capable of making something genuinely good?  
Also, if you used paid models or tools like **Cursor**, how much did you end up spending, and was it worth it?

comments.author: John_Champaign
comments.body:
Yes, I've made digital conversions of boardgames, implemented old arcade games, and created mods for commercial games (Mind Over Magic) all completely with AI.  

There's a big jump from the free versions to the paid versions, even lower tiers.  I use Anthropic's $100 plan, but I was getting good results when I was on their $20 plan.  If you're very price conscious, maybe just try the $20 plan for a month?

If projects are getting away from you, maybe try to build something smaller?  Keep reducing the size until you get something you're happy with.  As models improve (and you get better at game dev), increase the size of project that you work on.

comments.author: PhantomZenithOrigin
comments.body: On the subject of Qwen, and anything else for that matter remember: "You get what you pay for."

comments.author: Blake9712
comments.body: Ai is capable of doing most of the work although not good at assets and it wouldn’t exactly be a one shot experience. The issue is people underestimate the amount of work to polish a full gaming experience so if there are a few polished released games they’ll be hard to find between all the one shots or single month projects. Also figuring out how to efficiently get high quality assets and adding your own creativity etc is all rough. The ai losing track of its own code is part of it. Expect to feel like you aren’t making any progress for weeks because you’re chasing your tail. That’s part of it.

comments.author: ThisIsKappa
comments.body:
I've build https://partynight.host/ completely with ai. Opus 5.5 (code) combined with Elevenlabs (audio) and Codex (art). 

Workflow tends to be preparing a plan, optimizing the plan with Opus. Preparing an art direction with Codex. Decide the direction for audio for Elevenlabs. And prompt away, fine tune, correct and code audit regularly.

The better you know how to explain what you want the better the result.

comments.author: kopko222
comments.body:
Making a game right now. About 3-4 weeks in, its medieval autobattler / dungeon / party / guild sim. I am utilizing many subs as I hit the limits quite easily. 
Using AO (agent orchestrator) with many subs - codex, claude, cursor, opencode, command code, cline (last three are for deepseek 4.1 flash).
I have like 5-10 workers and using opus 5.5. as the game director. GPT sub is textures and assets. I think it will take me another 3-6 months to finish and polish. That is with campaign, voiceovers, sounds, free play etc etc... 
It takes time but without AI doing a project like this would take solo dev 2-3 years atleast.

comments.author: deReaLizedGames
comments.body:
It's 100% doable at this point, but like others said polishing the game is what actually takes the longest time. This is my first game, it took 9 months to get here:  
[https://store.steampowered.com/app/5073210/BoneHeads/](https://store.steampowered.com/app/5073210/BoneHeads/)

I've been working on my second game for 3 months. It's a much bigger project - full 3D, a deeper sword combat system, parkour mechanics, linear campaign levels, etc. It took 2 months just to build a system that enables AI to be actually competent at making linear levels. But this game is genuinely AA-quality now.

Opus 5.5 using Blender can now actually produce really good results in specific styles. Peoples' biggest mistake with AI is trying to fight against its constraints rather than lean into what it can make well. The human models it made and animated were pretty mediocre, but when I switched to a different type of character the game now looks genuinely AA level polish and the character animations are awesome. If you understand what AI is good and bad at, and design your game around that, it'll come out way better. The art style I ended up going with for this new game is no where near what I initially imagined, but Claude is so much better at it than other styles.

So when you see games left in infancy, that's really indicative of the developer abandoning the project rather than AI being unable to finish it. My first game has taken \~500-600 hours. I had a working prototype on the first day. Getting a primitive prototype with AI is the quick part, making that prototype good is what takes long. It also takes much more thinking, designing, and attention to detail. People get bored and move on. You have to be really passionate about your idea and enjoy the process to be able to follow through with it.

  
If you're having trouble with AI losing track of code I'd definitely switch to Claude, I've never had that issue with Claude. I've made both of my projects in pure HTML (my second game is in three.js) and it's been able to handle a huge code base no problem.

comments.author: BRaiNDED_Games
comments.body:
I made my game completely with AI in terms of code and assets. That said, echoing many others in here - the real time and effort is in the polish and details. I spent almost a full year from html concept in Gemini to full three.js 3D finished game with Claude code.

There were entire refactors, file restructuring, debugging, crazy hours playtesting and iterating, performance audits, etc. I did end up creating my own audio assets for the SFX (music was Suno though).

Final result is releasing in November on Steam - [Void Descent ](https://store.steampowered.com/app/4973630/Void_Descent/)

The key was to creat good processes and md files - once I setup a concise Claude.md and then supporting files like llms.txt (point it to the right files), arch.md (explains high level architecture and decisions along the way), and design.md (style guide to keep UI things reusable and standardized to the theme) everything got a lot smoother.

I also set up a lot of stuff to automate different builds since I have a web build, a steam build (windows and Linux separately) and then a demo build for each. It will automatically remove dev tools, gate demo features, package things up, then set everything back to dev mode.

In terms of cost I was using $20/mo claude pro CLI in cursor, a Suno subscription, and Magnific for 3d assets and image generation for reference.

So to summarize, AI is awesome but it doesn't replace actually putting in time and effort to make something of quality that is enjoyable to play for more than 5 mins.

Good luck on your projects!

comments.author: Felmeric
comments.body:
If game jam entries count as polished, released games then I have made a few. You can check their quality here: https://felmeric.itch.io/

I used Claude code for the coding, Google Gemini for some audio and to put together my ideas into a design doc and gamelabstudio.co for game ready art generation to make the most recent three, the candlelight heist used synty assets that I had bought from a humble bundle
 for the art.

The basic process for each was to work out the idea using Gemini, have it compile my thoughts and ideas into a design document and then take that to Claude code to actually implement it. That got me to the prototype stage, from there I iterated on that with Claude getting it to change things until the prototype started to look like my vision. At that point I got Claude to prompt 
gamelabstudio to generate the art. It took a few test images to get the style dialed in, then it the rest were easy to produce. 

As for pricing I have a Claude pro subscription, none of these took more than a month so less than $20 each. For the art, I have a 
gamelabstudio subscription but you could generate all the art for one of those games on their free trial credits if you knew what you wanted, or use a one time $20 payment for enough credits to generate the art for all three including learning with lots left over. Gemini is free.
